title: Leopold Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness piled back into AI bets last quarter after summer meltdown
excerpt: Leopold Aschenbrenner's lates bets were placed before the latest volatility gripped AI stocks and the tech trade since the highs of early October.

Situational Awareness wasn't scared off from betting on AI stocks after its summer meltdown.

The hedge fund run by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner was forced to sell off the bulk of its public equities portfolio to Citadel after a painful bout of volatility in the tech sector caused its holdings to plunge 67% and triggered a series of margin calls. It retained its stake in Anthropic, which is due to go public this week.

The firm released its quarterly 13F filing on November 16, revealing a tweaked strategy still rooted in AI bullishness. Throughout the quarter, it shifted focus from owning a wide range of AI common stocks to mostly call option exposure to AI-linked shares, though it took a large stake in Australian neocloud firm, SharonAI.

The cloud infrastructure company accounted for 28% of Situational Awareness' fund as of September 30, 2026. According to the 13F, the fund increased its position during the quarter by 2,674,823 shares.

While share prices jumped 12% on news of the hedge fund's stake on Tuesday, the stock has struggled this year, down about 28% year-to-date. Other neocloud stocks have battled high volatility recently as well, primarily due to debt concerns surrounding CoreWeave and broader fears related to the sustainability of the AI boom.

Other stocks and options tied to the AI trade that the fund loaded up on include Bloom Energy (24.7% of the portfolio), Nebius (21.1%), SanDisk (11.5%), and the Roundhill Memory ETF (8.9%).

The bets laid by the fund in the quarter were placed before the latest bout of market volatility that's rippled through the market since the highs of early October. SharonAI is down 54% since October 1.

Aschenbrenner's fund was clobbered by the swings in the AI trade in the middle of this year. The fund held assets worth $45 billion at its peak, falling to about $10 billion in a matter of days as a brutal sell-off in high-flying chip names triggered margin calls on levered positions.
